formation.title: The Kingdom of Benin
formation.text:
The Edo people have united under a single banner. Benin City, with its massive earthwork fortifications and broad avenues lined with guild workshops, stands as one of the great cities of West Africa. The Oba's palace dominates the skyline, its walls decorated with bronze plaques depicting the kingdom's history.

But the character of this new kingdom remains to be determined. Will the Oba assert absolute divine authority, concentrating all military and political power in the palace? Or will the kingdom's strength flow from its extraordinary guild system (the brass-casters of Igun Street, the ivory carvers, the blacksmiths) whose hereditary crafts have made Benin famous across the known world?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: The Oba is the kingdom; all power flows from the palace.

modifiers.name: Oba's Divine Authority
modifiers.text: The Oba rules as the divine embodiment of the Edo state, his word law, his palace the center of all power. The hereditary chiefs serve at his pleasure and the warrior guilds march at his command.

options.text: The guilds are the kingdom; their craft is our strength.

modifiers.name: City of Guilds
modifiers.text: Benin City thrives as a metropolis of organized artisan guilds, each mastering a hereditary craft under royal patronage. The brass-casters, ivory-carvers, leather-workers, and weavers form the economic and cultural backbone of the kingdom.

advances.name: Ogiso Legacy
advances.text: The traditions of the ancient Ogiso dynasty, the 'rulers of the sky,' form the spiritual foundation of Edo identity and ancestor worship.

advances.name: Iya Fortifications
advances.text: The massive earthwork moat-and-rampart system surrounding Benin City, begun under Oba Oguola, reaching heights of 18 meters and encircling the entire capital.

advances.name: Early Guild Organization
advances.text:
The first organization of Benin's artisan guilds under royal patronage, establishing the hereditary craft traditions that would define the kingdom's economy. The royal weavers, the Owina n'Ido, are counted among the oldest.

Available in: Owina n'Ido Ward

advances.name: Warrior Guild Tradition
advances.text: The organized warrior guilds of Benin, equipped with swords, spears, and shields of elephant or crocodile skin, famed for their discipline across the Guinea coast.

advances.name: Oral Histories of the Edo
advances.text: The rich oral traditions preserving the genealogy of the Obas, the deeds of ancestors, and the legal customs of the Edo people across generations.

advances.name: Ewuare's Reforms
advances.text: The sweeping political reforms of Oba Ewuare the Great, who centralized royal authority, reorganized the Uzama council, and transformed Benin into an imperial state.

event.title: The Legacy of Ewuare
event.text:
Oba Ewuare the Great transformed the Edo kingdom from a collection of loosely affiliated communities into an imperial state. He renamed the kingdom, rebuilt Benin City with broad streets radiating from the palace, reformed the political hierarchy by appointing the crown prince Edaiken as the seventh member of the Uzama council, and led military expeditions eastward against the Igala kingdom at Idah and westward to subdue the Yoruba towns of Owo and Idanre.

His campaigns expanded Benin's territory to over 5,000 square miles, creating a network of tributary relationships that fueled the kingdom's economy with levies of manpower and resources. But Ewuare was also a patron of arts and festivals, introducing the Igue ceremony and the guild of costume and bead workers.

Will we follow the path of Ewuare the conqueror, or Ewuare the builder?

options.text: His sword carved out our dominion.

modifiers.name: Ewuare the Conqueror
modifiers.text: Following the model of Oba Ewuare, the kingdom pursues aggressive expansion, subjugating neighboring peoples and demanding tribute in captives and resources.

modifiers.name: Ewuare the Builder
modifiers.text: Following the model of Oba Ewuare, the kingdom invests in rebuilding the capital, expanding the earthworks, and patronizing the arts and festivals that define Edo identity.

advances.name: Eben Sword Tradition
advances.text: The mastery of the eben, the traditional Edo short sword wielded by the warrior guilds in disciplined formations that foreign observers compared favorably to any in Guinea.

advances.name: Uzama Reform
advances.text: The reformation of the Uzama hereditary nobility, bringing the traditional kingmakers under firmer royal control and reducing their independent power.

advances.name: Regional Trade Networks
advances.text: Benin's role as a middle-trader between West African kingdoms, exchanging fish, salt, yams, cotton, and semi-precious stone beads across the Lower Niger region.

advances.name: Expanded Earthworks
advances.text: The extension of Benin's defensive earthworks into the outer city, creating an interconnecting system of moats and ramparts covering thousands of square kilometers.

advances.name: Court Arts Patronage
advances.text: The Oba's patronage of the hereditary artisan guilds, producing ivory carvings, bronze sculptures, coral bead work, and elaborately decorated textiles for the royal court.

advances.name: Portuguese Contact
advances.text: The arrival of Portuguese traders around 1486, opening Benin to Atlantic commerce and bringing new goods, technologies, and diplomatic relationships.

event.title: Arrival of the Portuguese
event.text:
Portuguese sailors have appeared on the coast near Benin City, bearing strange goods and stranger customs. Their delegations assiduously seek commercial treaties with the Oba, recognizing Benin as the most powerful polity in the region.

The Oba's position is strong. He has prohibited the sale of male slaves, he needs them for his own army, and imposed strict controls on all trade through royal monopoly. The Portuguese offer firearms, brass ingots for the bronze-casters, and access to distant markets. In return they seek pepper, ivory, cloth, and beads.

The question is not whether to trade, but what to prioritize. Shall we focus on acquiring European arms to strengthen our military, or on building lasting commercial relationships that will enrich the kingdom for generations?

options.text: Their weapons will make our warriors invincible.

modifiers.name: Portuguese Arms Trade
modifiers.text: European firearms and military supplies flow through Benin's ports, strengthening the kingdom's armed forces and enabling rapid military modernization.

options.text: Their markets will make our merchants wealthy.

modifiers.name: Portuguese Commercial Alliance
modifiers.text: Commercial ties with Portuguese merchants have opened new markets for Benin's pepper, ivory, and palm oil, enriching the kingdom's treasury and expanding its trade networks.

advances.name: Igun Eronmwon Mastery
advances.text:
The brass-casters of Igun Street achieve mastery of the lost-wax technique, producing the bronze plaques, portrait heads, and ceremonial objects that define Benin's artistic legacy.

Available in: Igun Street Workshop

event.title: Masters of the Lost-Wax
event.text:
The Igun Eronmwon, the guild of brass-casters on Igun Street, have reached an extraordinary level of mastery. Using the ancient lost-wax technique, where molten metal is poured into precisely carved wax and clay moulds, they produce portrait heads, commemorative plaques, and ceremonial objects of astonishing naturalism and detail.

Their work serves a political purpose as much as an artistic one. The bronze plaques that line the palace walls depict the history of the kingdom, the deeds of past Obas, and the proper order of the world. Every plaque is a statement of power, legitimacy, and cultural identity. The guild's hereditary membership ensures their secrets are preserved across generations, and their status as the highest-ranking artisan guild in Benin reflects the kingdom's understanding that artistic excellence is inseparable from political authority.

advances.name: Guild Warrior Tradition
advances.text: The maturation of Benin's organized warrior guilds into a disciplined military force, equipped with swords, spears, and poisoned arrows, capable of mobilizing 20,000 soldiers in a single day.

advances.name: Royal Trade Monopoly
advances.text:
The Oba's strict control over all foreign trade, creating royal monopolies on pepper, ivory, and palm oil that gave Benin a strong bargaining position with European merchants. Coral, too, is the Oba's alone to give.

Available in: Oba's Market House and Igun Street Workshop

advances.name: Pepper Export Trade
advances.text: The systematic export of pepper and ivory to European markets, with the Oba controlling prices and quantities to maximize the kingdom's profit.

advances.name: Lower Niger Administration
advances.text: The extension of Benin's administrative reach across the Lower Niger, establishing tributary relationships with neighboring polities through a combination of military force and diplomacy. War canoes carried the Oba's armies along the creeks and lagoons as far as Eko, the war camp that became Lagos.

advances.name: Iyoba Institution
advances.text: The establishment of the Iyoba, the Queen Mother, as a political institution with her own palace, court, and military regiment, a counterbalance to noble factions.

event.title: The Queen Mother's Court
event.text:
The institution of the Iyoba, the Queen Mother, has become a formidable pillar of Benin's political structure. The Iyoba commands her own palace, her own court, and most remarkably, her own military regiment. This is no mere ceremonial honor.

The Iyoba's regiment provides the Oba with a loyal military force separate from the warrior guilds and noble retinues, a counterbalance to any faction that might threaten royal authority. Her political influence extends through her own network of advisors and agents, giving the monarchy a second center of power that strengthens the whole structure.

The establishment of this institution represents a sophisticated understanding of governance, that concentrated power is less stable than distributed loyalty.

advances.name: Palace Societies
advances.text: The Iwebo, Iweguae, and Ibiwe palace societies that managed the Oba's wardrobe, regalia, and household respectively, forming a professional bureaucracy within the royal court.

advances.name: Ivory Export Mastery
advances.text:
The height of Benin's ivory trade, with skilled carvers producing elaborate tusks, armlets, and decorative objects for both domestic use and European markets.

Available in: Igbesanmwan Ward

advances.name: Firearms Adoption
advances.text: The integration of European firearms into Benin's military, initially through Portuguese trade and later through Dutch and British merchants.

advances.name: Benin City Planning
advances.text: The sophisticated urban organization of Benin City, with broad streets radiating from the Oba's palace, specialized guild quarters, and planned residential districts.

advances.name: Isekpokin Guild
advances.text: The Isekpokin guild of shield and leather-workers, producing the distinctive elephant and crocodile skin shields carried by Benin's warriors into battle.

advances.name: Absolute Monarchy
advances.text: The zenith of the Oba's absolute authority, with all aspects of political, economic, military, and religious life centered on the royal palace.

advances.name: Edo Musketeer Regiments
advances.text: The reorganization of Benin's blacksmith guilds to manufacture light firearms locally, reducing dependence on European imports for military hardware.

advances.name: Palm Oil Trade
advances.text: The expansion of palm oil exports as a major trade commodity, complementing the declining pepper and ivory trades in the later period.

advances.name: European Diplomacy
advances.text: Benin's sophisticated diplomatic maneuvering between competing European powers, Portuguese, Dutch, and British, playing rivals against each other to maintain independence.

advances.name: Defensive Warfare Doctrine
advances.text: The kingdom's shift toward defensive military strategy, leveraging the massive earthwork fortifications and knowledge of local terrain against foreign incursions.

advances.name: Military Manpower Reserve
advances.text: The Oba's prohibition on selling male slaves, preserving the kingdom's manpower for its own military needs and ensuring a large reserve of warriors.

advances.name: Guild Codification
advances.text: The formal codification of guild traditions, techniques, and hereditary rights, preserving centuries of accumulated knowledge in brass-casting, ivory-carving, and textile production.

advances.name: Local Firearms Manufacture
advances.text:
The development of indigenous firearms production by reorganized blacksmith guilds, achieving partial independence from European arms imports.

Available in: Igun Street Workshop

advances.name: Sovereignty Defense
advances.text: The kingdom's determined resistance to European colonial encroachment, drawing on centuries of military tradition and the natural advantages of the earthwork fortifications.

advances.name: Trade Diversification
advances.text: The diversification of Benin's export economy beyond the traditional pepper, ivory, and palm oil trade to include manufactured goods and processed materials.

advances.name: Cultural Resilience
advances.text: The enduring strength of Edo cultural identity, the guild traditions, the Oba's rituals, the bronze-casting legacy, persisting through centuries of external pressure and change.

destiny.name: Destiny of Benin
destiny.text: The Kingdom of Benin has been forged. Now the Oba must decide the path forward, will this kingdom become a military empire or a guild-powered economic powerhouse?

event.title: Destiny of the Kingdom
event.text:
The Kingdom of Benin stands at a crossroads. The Oba's palace rises above a city of broad avenues and guild workshops, its walls adorned with bronze plaques depicting the deeds of past rulers. The earthwork fortifications stretch for miles in every direction.

But a stable kingdom is merely a beginning. The path chosen at the kingdom's founding now beckons, whether through the sword or through the workshop, Benin's destiny awaits.

options.text: Our destiny is written in bronze.

destiny.name: Western Wars
destiny.text: Subjugate the Yoruba heartland at Oyo-Ile and seize the trading port of Calabar to establish the Oba's military dominion over the Lower Niger and beyond. The warrior guilds must have their camp: take Eko, where the Oba's army made its war camp, or build them barracks.

conditions.text: Own Ọ̀yọ́ Ile, or a subject owns it
Own Calabar, or a subject owns it
We hold Eko, the war camp of the Oba, or one of our locations has a Warrior Guild Barracks

event.title: The Western Campaigns
event.text:
The Oba's warriors have marched west and east, bringing the ancient city of Oyo-Ile and the trading port of Calabar under Benin's authority. The Yoruba and the peoples of the Cross River now acknowledge the Oba's supremacy.

These conquests echo the campaigns of Oba Ewuare himself, who first extended Benin's power beyond its heartland. The warrior guilds have proven their worth, and the kingdom's borders now encompass a vast territory of diverse peoples and resources.

destiny.name: Northern Reach
destiny.text: Extend the Oba's power into the Hausa states by conquering Kano and the Bornu capital of Ngazargamu, bringing the great trading cities of the Sahel under Benin's authority. The warriors of the eben sword must be trained.

conditions.text: Own Kano, or a subject owns it
Own Ngazargamu, or a subject owns it

event.title: Dominion Over the North
event.text:
The great walled cities of the Hausa, Kano with its dye pits and leather markets, and Ngazargamu, capital of the Bornu empire, now fly the banner of Benin. The Oba's armies have crossed the vast savanna to bring these wealthy trading centers under his authority.

This is an empire of unprecedented scope for a kingdom born in the forests of the Lower Niger. The question now is how to consolidate these conquests. Shall the Oba forge his warriors into an even more fearsome fighting force, or establish a system of tributaries that enriches the kingdom while pacifying the conquered?

options.text: Our warriors are the finest in West Africa.

modifiers.name: Warriors of the Oba
modifiers.text: The Oba's warrior guilds have been forged into the most fearsome fighting force in West Africa, their morale unbreakable and their tactics refined through campaigns across the savanna. The men kept under arms are missed on the farms.

options.text: Let the tributaries fill our coffers.

modifiers.name: Tributaries of the Oba
modifiers.text: A vast network of tributary states sustains the Oba's military machine, reducing the cost of maintaining armies while mercenary companies supplement the warrior guilds.

destiny.name: Imperial Dominion
destiny.text: The Oba's armies must reach the gold fields of Kumasi and the legendary city of Timbuktu, establishing Benin as the supreme power of West Africa. The guild warriors must be organized.

conditions.text: Own Kumasi, or a subject owns it
Own Timbuktu, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Empire of the Oba
event.text:
From the gold fields of Kumasi to the legendary libraries of Timbuktu, the Oba's dominion stretches across the breadth of West Africa. No ruler in the region's history has commanded such vast territory, a military achievement that would astonish the Portuguese traders who first came seeking pepper and ivory.

The bronze plaques in the palace must be extended to record these triumphs. But the nature of this empire's military strength remains to be decided. Shall the Oba invest in a professional imperial army drawing on all the conquered peoples, or pursue a grand strategy of diplomatic intimidation backed by overwhelming force?

options.text: Build the greatest army West Africa has seen.

modifiers.name: The Oba's Imperial Army
modifiers.text: A professional imperial army drawing cavalry and artillery from across the conquered territories, unified under the Oba's supreme command into a force of devastating speed and power.

options.text: Let our reputation precede our armies.

modifiers.name: Grand Strategy of Benin
modifiers.text: The Oba's reputation for overwhelming military force precedes his armies, enabling rapid annexation of rivals while an extensive spy network protects the empire from internal threats.

destiny.name: Guild Wealth
destiny.text: The guild system must generate enough surplus to fill the Oba's treasury, and the royal weavers of the Owina n'Ido must have their ward in Benin City.

conditions.text: We own Benin City and it has an Owina n'Ido Ward

event.title: The Treasury of the Guilds
event.text:
The guild system has generated extraordinary wealth. The brass-casters, ivory-carvers, cloth-weavers, and leather-workers produce goods that command premium prices in markets near and far. The Oba's treasury overflows with the proceeds of royal monopoly trade, and the ward of the royal weavers turns out cloth that no other court in the region can match.

Benin City thrives as a metropolis of organized industry, where every street belongs to a guild and every craft is perfected across generations.

options.text: The guilds are the wealth of the kingdom.

destiny.name: Artisan Power
destiny.text: The guild wards must raise the development of Benin City to 14 while ivory, worked by the kingdom's master carvers, flows through the capital's markets to distant lands.

conditions.text: Benin is owned and has development of at least 14

children.text: Ivory is produced in the market
Ivory is traded in the market

event.title: Masters of Their Craft
event.text:
The guild workshops have become engines of development, driving growth across the kingdom. Ivory carved by Benin's master artisans flows through the capital's markets to buyers across the known world. The kingdom's development has outpaced its neighbors, built on the foundation of hereditary craft knowledge refined over centuries.

The guilds now stand at a crossroads of their own. Some guild masters push for ever-greater artistic refinement, literacy, education, the preservation of techniques in writing rather than memory alone. Others see the future in commerce, expanding diplomatic ties, opening new markets, leveraging the guild system's wealth to project influence abroad.

options.text: Mastery of craft demands mastery of knowledge.

modifiers.name: Master Craftsmen
modifiers.text: The guild masters have elevated their hereditary crafts to the level of high art, driving cultural influence and literacy across the kingdom, though the focus on workshop over warfield makes campaigning costlier.

options.text: Our merchants shall carry guild wares to every port.

modifiers.name: Merchant Princes
modifiers.text: A new class of wealthy guild traders has emerged, wielding diplomatic influence and financial acumen that opens markets and forges alliances across the trading world.

destiny.name: Guild Imperium
destiny.text: Benin's guild system must reach its apex: a wealthy kingdom whose capital has grown to a development of 19, twice what it was, and which holds the sacred city of Ife, where the brass-casting tradition originated in the art of the Yoruba ancestors.

conditions.text: Benin is owned and has development of at least 19
Own Ifẹ̀, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Guild Imperium
event.text:
Benin has achieved what no other West African kingdom has managed, an empire built not primarily on conquest but on the productive power of its guild system. The kingdom's wealth, its cultural influence, its diplomatic connections all flow from the workshops of Igun Street and their counterparts across the realm.

The sacred city of Ife, where the artistic tradition of bronze-casting first took root among the Yoruba, now acknowledges Benin's cultural supremacy. The circle is complete, from Ife the art came, and to Ife's masters Benin now stands as proof of what that art can build.

How shall this imperium express its power in the years ahead?

options.text: Build a city that rivals any in the world.

modifiers.name: Artisan Metropolis
modifiers.text: Benin City has grown into a true metropolis of organized industry, where efficient urban planning and powerful trade centers draw commerce from distant lands.

options.text: Let our culture reach every shore.

modifiers.name: Cultural Renaissance
modifiers.text: The guild system's wealth has funded a maritime expansion, building ships and training sailors to carry Benin's famous artisan goods to ports along the entire West African coast and beyond.

units.name: Eben Warriors
units.text: Disciplined Edo sword infantry wielding the traditional eben short sword and shields of elephant skin. Foreign observers noted their organization surpassed any other force on the Guinea coast.

units.name: Guild Warriors
units.text: The organized warrior guilds of Benin, equipped with swords, spears, and poisoned arrows. Capable of being mobilized twenty thousand strong in a single day at the Oba's command.

units.name: Edo War Canoe
units.text: A great dugout hewn from a single forest tree, paddled by dozens of men and packed with warriors. Fleets of them carried the Oba's armies through the creeks and lagoons to the war camp at Eko. Swift in shoal water where no ship can follow, but a poor platform for guns.

units.name: Iyoba Guard
units.text: The Queen Mother's own regiment, a loyal military force personally commanded by the Iyoba. They serve as a counterbalance to the noble retinues and warrior guild factions.

units.name: Edo Musketeers
units.text: Benin's locally-armed musketeer regiments, equipped with firearms manufactured by the kingdom's reorganized blacksmith guilds, reducing dependence on European arms imports.

buildings.name: Igun Street Workshop
buildings.text: The workshops of the Igun Eronmwon guild on Igun Street, where hereditary brass-casters produce the famous Benin Bronzes using the ancient lost-wax technique.

buildings.name: Isekpokin Ward
buildings.text: The quarter of the Isekpokin, the hereditary guild of leather workers. Here hides of forest game are cured and stretched over frames to make the tall shields of the warrior guilds, along with quivers, sheaths and the leather fans of the court.

buildings.name: Igbesanmwan Ward
buildings.text: The quarter of the Igbesanmwan, the hereditary guild of ivory carvers. They work for the Oba, to whom one tusk of every elephant killed is owed.

buildings.name: Owina n'Ido Ward
buildings.text: The quarter of the Owina n'Ido, the royal weavers. Their guild is held to be as old as the Ogiso kings, and the patterned cloths of the court are theirs alone to weave.

buildings.name: Oba's Market House
buildings.text: A royal trade house where all foreign commerce passes under the Oba's monopoly. Pepper, ivory, and palm oil are weighed, taxed, and allocated by royal agents.

buildings.name: Iya Earthwork
buildings.text: A section of the massive moat-and-rampart system that once encircled Benin City and its surrounding territories, reaching heights of 18 meters with interconnecting circles of ditches and dump ramparts.

buildings.name: Warrior Guild Barracks
buildings.text: Training grounds and armories for the organized warrior guilds, where soldiers drill in the use of the eben sword, spear, and bow under the direction of hereditary war chiefs.

buildings.name: Ogiso Ancestral Shrine
buildings.text: A shrine dedicated to the ancient Ogiso dynasty, the 'rulers of the sky' who preceded the Oba dynasty and whose spiritual legacy underpins Edo religious practice and cultural identity.

buildings.name: Storyteller's Hall
buildings.text: A gathering place where griots and oral historians preserve and transmit the genealogies, laws, and epic narratives of the Edo people through the art of storytelling.

buildings.name: Oba's Administrative Hall
buildings.text: A hall of governance where the Oba's appointed officials manage tribute collection, territorial administration, and the complex hierarchy of hereditary and appointed chiefs.

buildings.name: Palace Society Hall
buildings.text: The headquarters of the Iwebo, Iweguae, and Ibiwe palace societies, professional organizations managing the royal household's wardrobe, regalia, and ceremonial functions.

buildings.name: Oba's Court
buildings.text: The magnificent royal court of the Oba, center of political authority, cultural patronage, and diplomatic reception for the entire kingdom.

buildings.name: Oba's War Palace
buildings.text: The fortified command center of the Oba's imperial army, combining the traditional palace architecture of Benin with military barracks, armories, and war councils drawn from the conquered territories.

buildings.name: Guild Masters' Hall
buildings.text: The grand assembly hall of Benin's guild masters, where the heads of every hereditary craft guild meet to coordinate production, set quality standards, and manage the vast trade networks that sustain the kingdom's wealth.

list.name: Uzama Nihinron
list.text: The seven hereditary kingmaker chiefs of metropolitan Benin (Oliha, Edohen, Ezomo, Ero, Eholo n'Ire, Oloton, and Ihaza) whose offices predate the Oba dynasty itself. Tradition holds that the Uzama invited Oranmiyan of Ife to send a son to rule them around 1200, founding the line of Eweka I. They retain the constitutional right to instal each new Oba: no king's accession is legitimate without the coronation at Usama, where the Oliha places the beaded crown on his head. After Ewuare's reforms of c.1440 they were stripped of administrative power but kept the kingmaker role, making them a permanent counterweight to royal authority.

list.name: Eghaevbo n'Ogbe
list.text: Ewuare the Great (r. c.1440-1473) reorganized Benin governance around three palace societies, each headquartered in its own quarter of the Oba's residence: Iwebo (chiefs of regalia, brass, and ivory), Iweguae (chiefs of the king's person and household), and Ibiwe (chiefs of the harem and royal children). Each society admitted men by royal appointment rather than birth; their titled members collectively formed the Eghaevbo n'Ogbe, the palace chiefs, a body deliberately constructed to give the Oba an administrative arm independent of the Uzama and the town-chiefs.

list.name: Igun-Eronmwon Brass Guild
list.text: The Brass-Casters' Guild of Igun Street in Benin City held the royal monopoly on the lost-wax casting of the commemorative plaques, heads, and figurines now known as the Benin Bronzes (in fact a leaded brass alloy from the trans-Saharan and later Atlantic copper trade). The guild master, the Inneh n'Igun-Eronmwon, ranked as a senior chief of the Iwebo. A parallel guild, the Igbesanmwan ivory carvers, supplied the carved tusks of royal altars. Together they produced the durable record of dynastic history that the Edo court considered its archive in metal and ivory.

list.name: Igue Festival
list.text: Codified by Ewuare around 1440 and still observed in modern Benin, the Igue is the annual festival of royal renewal. The cycle of rites (Ague, Otue, Ugie Erha Oba, Ugie Oro, Igue proper, and the closing Iron-Day) runs for several weeks each December and requires every titled chief in the realm to attend the Oba's palace, present tribute, swear the year's oath of loyalty, and undergo the propitiatory sacrifices that renew the king's mystical authority. Igue is simultaneously a calendrical ritual, a tribute assessment, and a constitutional review: a chief who fails to appear is treated as having broken his oath of fealty.

list.name: Iyase n'Ode
list.text: The senior of the Eghaevbo n'Ore (the town chiefs) and the constitutional war-commander of the Edo state, the Iyase leads the Oba's armies in the field while the king himself remains ritually within the palace. The office combines operational command, recruitment of the regional levies, and the right to refuse a war the Iyase judges unwinnable: a check that produced the 18th-century revolts of Iyase n'Ode and Iyase Esebo. The title's ambivalence (the throne's chief general and the throne's most likely military rebel) captures the Edo state's tension between sacred kingship and battlefield reality.

list.name: Ologbo'na Residency
list.text: As Benin's empire expanded westward and northward in the 15th and 16th centuries under Ewuare, Ozolua, and Esigie, the Oba posted Ologbo'na (called Olaen in some western districts), royal residents drawn from the palace societies, to the courts of Akure, Owo, the Ekiti towns, Mahin, and the Edo coastal foundations that became Lagos. Each Ologbo'na assessed annual tribute of slaves, ivory, cloth, and salt and forwarded remittances to Benin City. The residency made Benin's tributary system functional, but extortion documented in the Akure and Owo records generated the chronic resentment that erupted in 17th-century revolts.
